subject: Vocabulary
topic: Proverbs III — Meaning, Application and Confusable Near-Meanings (W13 B1)

questions.stem: What is the correct meaning of the proverb: 'A STITCH IN TIME SAVES NINE'?

options.option_text: One should learn embroidery before attempting complex crafts
Acting promptly to correct a small problem will prevent a much larger problem later
Nine people cannot solve a problem that one expert can
Precision is more important than speed in all tasks

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'A STITCH IN TIME SAVES NINE' = if you repair a small tear in cloth now (one stitch), you prevent a larger tear that would require nine stitches later. Figuratively: act now on a small problem to avoid a larger problem later; timely action prevents greater future effort. Trap: 'precision more important than speed' = misreads the proverb as being about quality vs speed; the message is about TIMING of action, not quality.

questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates 'FOOLS RUSH IN WHERE ANGELS FEAR TO TREAD'?

options.option_text: A skilled surgeon performing a routine procedure for the hundredth time
An inexperienced investor putting his savings into a highly volatile investment that experts avoid
A coward who refuses to face any danger
A child asking questions that adults are too polite to raise

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'FOOLS RUSH IN WHERE ANGELS FEAR TO TREAD' = reckless or inexperienced people attempt things that wiser, more experienced people avoid. B illustrates this precisely: an inexperienced investor takes a risk (volatile investment) that experts (angels/wise people) avoid = fool rushing in. Origin: Alexander Pope's 'Essay on Criticism' (1711). Trap: 'coward who refuses danger' = describes timidity, not the reckless overconfidence the proverb criticises; 'child asking questions' = describes innocent openness, not the reckless disregard for risk.

questions.stem: What does 'THE PROOF OF THE PUDDING IS IN THE EATING' mean?

options.option_text: One should taste food before serving it to guests
The real value of something can only be judged by trying or using it, not by its appearance
Actions speak louder than words
Practice makes a person perfect over time

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'THE PROOF OF THE PUDDING IS IN THE EATING' = the true quality of something can only be judged by actually experiencing or using it, not by its appearance or how it is described. A pudding may look beautiful but taste terrible (or vice versa) — you only know by eating it. Similarly: evaluate products, plans, or people by results, not promises. Trap: 'actions speak louder than words' = a related meaning but emphasises behaviour vs talk, not the evaluation-through-experience angle; 'practice makes perfect' = about improvement through repetition, not evaluation.

questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates 'ALL THAT GLITTERS IS NOT GOLD'?

options.option_text: A mining company finds gold ore but it turns out to be pyrite (fool's gold)
A person earns a lot of money but is very unhappy
A fashionable product becomes worthless once the trend passes
An athlete wins a gold medal that later gets revoked for doping

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'ALL THAT GLITTERS IS NOT GOLD' = not everything that looks valuable or attractive is actually valuable; appearances can be deceptive. A: Pyrite (fool's gold) glitters like gold but is not gold — perfect literal AND figurative illustration of the proverb. Origin: Shakespeare's 'The Merchant of Venice'. Trap: B (money but unhappy) = illustrates 'money doesn't buy happiness' (different proverb); C (trend passing) = illustrates 'all things pass' or 'fashion is fleeting'; D (medal revoked) = illustrates 'cheating doesn't pay' or 'ill-gotten gains'. Only A directly illustrates the glitter-vs-genuine-gold contrast.

questions.stem: What does 'EMPTY VESSELS MAKE THE MOST NOISE' mean?

options.option_text: Hollow objects produce louder sounds than solid ones
People with the least knowledge or ability are often the most loud and boastful
A quiet person is usually hiding something important
Confidence comes from knowing that you are right

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'EMPTY VESSELS MAKE THE MOST NOISE' = those with the least knowledge, substance or wisdom tend to be the loudest and most boastful; they try to compensate for their emptiness by making noise. Figuratively: shallow or ignorant people talk the most. Origin: the physical truth (empty drums/pots are louder when struck than full ones) becomes a metaphor for intellectual emptiness. Trap: 'hollow objects are louder' = the literal (non-figurative) reading; the proverb is entirely figurative about human behaviour.

questions.stem: What does 'DON'T BIT THE HAND THAT FEEDS YOU' mean?

options.option_text: Be careful when accepting food from strangers
Do not harm or show ingratitude towards someone who helps or supports you
A dog that bites its owner is dangerous and should be removed
Be aggressive only when your survival is threatened

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'DON'T BITE THE HAND THAT FEEDS YOU' = do not act against or harm those who provide for or support you; do not show ingratitude to your benefactor. The image: a dog that bites the hand of the person feeding it is being self-destructively ungrateful. Figuratively: criticising or harming your employer, patron, government or benefactor is foolish and ungrateful. Trap: 'careful when accepting food' = literal misread; 'be aggressive only when threatened' = about self-defence, not about ingratitude.

questions.stem: Which proverb means the same as 'NECESSITY IS THE MOTHER OF INVENTION'?

options.option_text: Where there's a will, there's a way
Need teaches a man many things
Invention is the master of commerce
Work is worship

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'NECESSITY IS THE MOTHER OF INVENTION' = urgent need compels people to find creative solutions; necessity drives innovation. 'Need teaches a man many things' = when faced with necessity, people learn and invent — the same essential message. Trap: 'where there's a will, there's a way' = emphasises determination and willpower, not the COMPULSION of need/necessity (you choose to try vs you are forced by need); 'work is worship' = about dedication to work, not about need driving innovation.

questions.stem: What does 'EVERY CLOUD HAS A SILVER LINING' convey?

options.option_text: Rain is always followed by sunshine
Every difficult or negative situation has some positive or hopeful aspect
Hard work is always rewarded in the end
Good things come to those who wait patiently

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'EVERY CLOUD HAS A SILVER LINING' = in every bad, dark or challenging situation, there is always something positive to find; even in the worst circumstances, a ray of hope exists. A dark cloud (bad situation) has a bright silver edge (positive aspect) when the sun shines behind it. Trap: 'rain always followed by sunshine' = a meteorological fact, not the figurative message (it's about finding the positive in negatives, not just that bad weather ends); 'hard work is rewarded' = different proverb ('no pain, no gain').

questions.stem: Which situation BEST illustrates 'BEGGARS CAN'T BE CHOOSERS'?

options.option_text: A wealthy executive rejects a job offer because the salary is insufficient
A drought-stricken farmer accepts inferior seeds because no better seeds are available
A charity refuses to accept donated goods that do not meet quality standards
A voter selects the least bad candidate in an election with no ideal option

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'BEGGARS CAN'T BE CHOOSERS' = people who are in desperate need cannot afford to be selective; those who depend on others' help must accept what is offered. B perfectly illustrates this: the drought-stricken (desperate) farmer has no choice but to accept inferior seeds — he is in no position to demand better. Trap: A = wealthy executive rejects offer = a CHOOSER who is not a beggar (opposite situation); C = charity rejecting donations = choosers with standards (not desperate); D = voter choosing 'least bad' = deciding between options, not accepting what's given without choice.

questions.stem: What does 'THE PEN IS MIGHTIER THAN THE SWORD' convey?

options.option_text: Writing equipment is more expensive to manufacture than weaponry
A poet is safer than a soldier in battle
Written words and ideas have more lasting power and influence than physical force
Diplomacy always succeeds where military action fails

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'THE PEN IS MIGHTIER THAN THE SWORD' = writing, communication, knowledge and ideas are more powerful and have more lasting impact than physical violence or military power. Origin: Edward Bulwer-Lytton's play 'Richelieu' (1839). Use: 'A newspaper editorial can topple a government; that is why the pen is mightier than the sword.' Trap: 'diplomacy always succeeds' = a related but narrower claim; the proverb is specifically about the power of words/writing over physical force, not diplomacy in particular; 'poet safer than soldier' = a literal misread.
